'*Anaya*' occurs in the sense of non-increase (ruin). The formation of words should be understood by the characteristics of linguistics (*nirutti*) in all places. Paccekabuddhas know the benefits performed over many hundreds of thousands of aeons; they make the benefits manifest by remembering them, by accepting material offerings (*āmisa*) to inspire mindfulness, and so forth; likewise, they respectfully perform what should be done for those in distress. The Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (*Sammāsambuddha*), however, knows the benefits performed even over incalculable and immeasurable periods, as well as the strong supporting conditions for the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*); He makes them manifest, and like the speed of a lion king, He respectfully delivers the Dhamma teaching in all places. 'Noble state' (*ariyabhāva*) refers to those states of the paths and fruits by association with which one is called 'Noble' (*ariya*). The states that make one Noble are the contemplation of impermanence (*anicca*) and so forth, or the states of impermanence and so forth that are being contemplated.

'*Sotāni*' (streams) are the currents of craving, view, defilement, misconduct, and ignorance. After saying, "I declare the restraint of the streams," by the statement, "These are closed by wisdom," it is understood that the restraint and closing of the streams is the knowledge of total eradication (*samuccheda-ñāṇa*). '*Khanti*' is endurance; it refers to the mental aggregates functioning in that way. Some say it is wisdom, or it is simply non-hatred (*adosa*). It is the restraint of bodily and verbal misconduct called immorality, and of negligence (*pamāda*) called lapse of mindfulness, of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), of displeasure (*domanassa*), and of the evil states of impatience, lack of knowledge, and laziness. '*Anupekkhā*' means not turning away from formations, meaning attachment (*ālayatā*). Being contrary to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is called the stability of Dhamma (*dhammaṭṭhiti*), is the grasping of eternalism or annihilationism, or the delusion (*moha*) that covers that dependent origination. Being contrary to Nibbāna is delighting in formations, or the delusion that covers Nibbāna. 'Grasping the sign of formations' (*saṅkhāranimittaggāha*) refers to that defilement because of which, not having been abandoned, *vipassanā* cannot let go of the sign of formations. Alternatively, it is the transcending or abandoning of the grasping of the sign of formations.

The construction should be understood as: abandoning by way of absolute non-occurrence because the four Noble Paths have been developed. By what is it abandoned? It is understood that it is abandoned by the Noble Paths themselves, through the statement of non-occurrence due to the development of those paths. In the term 'on the side of origination' (*samudayapakkhika*), since all four paths are the realization of the Four Noble Truths, by those paths...
163:
Defilements such as wrong view are called "samudayapakkhika" (allied with the origin) because they are abandoned together with the respective origins (craving/greed) that are to be abandoned, because they share the same nature as the origin, and because all defilements are stated to be the origin in the Saccavibhaṅga.

The removal of the distorted occurrence of body, speech, and mind, or the factor that removes them, is called vinaya. Alternatively, that which leads to the destruction of bodily misconduct and so forth, or the factor that leads to such destruction, is called vinaya. Alternatively, the act of cutting off the crooked occurrence of body, speech, and mind and leading them to straightness is called vinayana.

"Esese" means this (the discipline of the noble ones) is that very (discipline of the good persons); it means they are not different in meaning. "Tajjāta" means, in terms of meaning, having that very nature. A good person (sappurisa) has the nature of a noble one (ariya), and a noble one has the nature of a good person.

"Adwaya" means the absence of duality. Just as one might see the unity of color and flame by taking the color itself as the "flame" or the flame itself as the "color," so too should one be understood as seeing the unity of the self and form by taking the conceived self as "form" or the perceived form as "self." In this (personality belief), although the occurrence of "form is the self" (as a self distinct from form) does not exist, the grasping of form as self occurs just like the grasping of color in a flame. The similes are stated only by way of illustrating the grasping of non-difference and so forth; they are not stated to show the existence of the self like color, nor to show the non-existence of color like the self.

"Sarīranipphattiyā" relates to the completion of the body. "Vicikicchā" (doubt) is so called because one becomes weary while investigating when unable to decide. By the phrase "idappaccayānaṃ bhāvo," the nature of birth (jāti) and so forth is meant. Alternatively, it refers to the capacity of birth and so forth to produce aging, death, and so forth. Since that capacity does not exist apart from birth and so forth, "idappaccayatā" (specific conditionality) is a designation for birth and so forth themselves.

In this (context of what is abandoned by vision), future defilements are called "tadekaṭṭhakilesa" (defilements standing on the same ground). To show those future defilements, the passage beginning with "imissā ca pāḷiyā" is undertaken. "Sahajekaṭṭhavasena" is understood in meaning as "by way of standing on the same ground as conascent" with the wrong view that has arisen in that (consciousness associated with wrong view), thus standing in a single consciousness. "Taṃsampayutto" also fits the meaning as "associated with those fetter-defilements." Likewise, because those fetter-defilements are the cause of origin (samuṭṭhāna) for this (kamma), it is called "taṃsamuṭṭhāna." Because of the existence of the aggregates associated with defilements that do not receive the name of fetters (such as sloth and restlessness) and the kammas caused by those defilements, the connection is made only with defilements.

"Saṃyojanādīnaṃ viya" means like (the abandonment of) the aforementioned fetters, defilements standing on the same ground, and so forth. "Tehi" means by the path of vision (dassana-magga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-magga). Formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāravijñāṇa) means...
164:
Considering wholesome and unwholesome states and mind-matter as resultants (vipāka), he said, "The abandonment of the wholesome and so forth is also permitted."

"Hetū ceva" means that in the compound word "pahatabbāhetukā," it intends to express the meaning of the compound word partially. In this text, when it is said by the first method, "These states have causes to be abandoned by vision," the restriction is evident that only these states have causes to be abandoned by vision, and not others. However, the restriction that these states only have causes to be abandoned by vision is not evident. Therefore, because the delusion associated with skeptical doubt has no associated root-cause (hetu), the status of these states as having causes to be abandoned by vision is not fixed. Thus, the first method has a meaning that needs to be explained. Therefore, having set aside those that have causes to be abandoned by vision by way of the phenomena (dhamma) according to the first method, the second method is taught to set them aside by way of meaning.

Exalted states (mahaggata) such as the supernormal powers (iddhividha) also occur. Exalted states having the immeasurable as their object are those states associated with the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa).

Kammas that are joined with the immediate result of death, or kammas that have the immediate result of death as their purpose, or kammas that have the habit of producing the immediate result of death are called "ānantarika" (immediate). Because those immediate kammas have results that cannot be prevented by opposing kammas, they are free from obstacles; therefore, it is said, "They give results without obstacles." The formation of the word "ānantarika" should be understood by way of linguistics (nirutti) as kammas that have no obstacles (anantarāya). In the phrase "ekasmimpi," the word "pi" shows the meaning that even if many kammas are accumulated, there is no need to say they are "ānantarika" (as if they were different). There is no mutual exclusion among those immediate kammas because they are not opposites. Their non-opposition is due to having similar results and providing mutual support.

"There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings"—such a doctrine is called the doctrine of non-causality (ahetukavāda). "For one who acts, for one who causes to act, for one who cuts, for one who causes to cut... though one acts, no evil is done"—such a doctrine is called the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda). "There is no result of giving"—such a doctrine is called the doctrine of nihilism (natthikavāda). Among these three doctrines, the first, the doctrine of non-causality, denies the cause of bondage and liberation in saṃsāra. The second doctrine denies kamma. The third doctrine denies the resultant (vipāka). This is the distinction between these doctrines. "Taṃ" refers to the fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) such as non-causality, and not to the view that has not yet reached the state of being fixed.

"Paccayāṭṭhena" should be understood as being by way of the condition distinguished by association, known as the path-condition (magga-paccaya). In this first method, the exclusion of the path-factors refers to those that are devoid of the status of path-condition...
165:
The path-factors are excluded in order to show the states that have path-factors as their cause (magghetuka) but are distinct from the path-condition. By this exclusion, He defines the magghetuka states without mixing them with the eight path-factors.

If someone were to say: "Even when excluding each path-factor individually, the statement 'excluding the path-factors' is appropriate regarding the magghetuka nature of the states associated with those respective path-factors." If this were so, then in this first method, as in the third method, the word "excluding" should not have been spoken; yet it was indeed spoken. Therefore, the meaning should be understood only by the method already stated in the Commentary. For this method has the purpose of showing the distinction between the states that are path-factors and the associated states that are not path-factors. It means the intention is toward the remaining path-factors that were excluded in the first method. The magghetuka nature of states such as contact (phassa) and so on is already established in the first method.

In the third method, the sahetuka (having causes) nature of Sammādiṭṭhi (Right View), which was excluded in the second method, is also shown. How is it shown? For a person endowed with the Noble Path, He does not say, "Non-greed and non-hatred, these states are path-causes (magghetu)"; rather, He separately shows the path-causes such as Sammādiṭṭhi by saying, "Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, these states are path-causes," and then separately shows the magghetuka states by saying, "the aggregate of consciousness associated with those causes," etc. Because of this, would it not mean that the magghetuka nature of Sammādiṭṭhi, which is spoken of as "amoha (non-delusion) among the path-causes," is not shown? It is not that it is not shown; it is indeed shown.

For example, after showing the three fetters (saṃyojana), He specifies the causes to be abandoned by saying, "Greed, hatred, and delusion existing therein are the causes to be abandoned by vision (dassanena pahātabba-hetu)"; then, with the words "and the defilements existing therein," etc., He shows that greed, hatred, and delusion—which are conascent, associated with one another, and belong to the aggregate of mental formations—are states having causes to be abandoned by vision (dassanena pahātabba-hetuka). Similarly, in this third method, although He concludes by saying, "Non-greed and so on, these states are path-causes," they are already shown as magghetuka by the phrase "the aggregate of mental formations associated with those causes," because they are associated mental formations. Therefore, the demonstration of the magghetuka nature of Sammādiṭṭhi, which is called amoha, is already accomplished.

If the third method were for the purpose of showing the magghetuka nature of Sammādiṭṭhi through its association with non-greed and non-hatred—showing the magghetuka nature of only non-greed and non-hatred (which are distinct from that Sammādiṭṭhi called "both path and cause" in the second method) by a specific figurative method (pariyāya) not shared with amoha—then He should have preached, "For a person endowed with the Noble Path, non-greed and non-hatred, these states are path-causes," and so on. However, since the magghetuka nature of those three causes is possible through another common figurative method called "magghetu," He shows all those causes as "magghetu" and...
166:
The third method has the purpose of showing the magghetuka nature of the causes associated with those three causes, as well as other states such as contact (phassa), etc., which are distinct from the three causes. Therefore, in that third method (or in the sense of magghetu), "amoha" is also spoken. Indeed, it should be noted that this amoha is not a non-magghetu; it is certainly a magghetu. These three methods should be understood as "presentation by way of meaning" (atthato nikkhepa) because they are laid down by the power of specific conceptual definitions. Alternatively, preaching by way of the actual form (sarūpa) is called "presentation by way of nature" (dhammato nikkhepa), while preaching by way of meaning is called "presentation by way of meaning" (atthato nikkhepa); such an application of meaning is also possible. Among those methods, the second and third methods are dhammato nikkhepa by way of showing the causes and the states having causes (hetu-hetumanta) in their actual form. The first method is atthato nikkhepa because it does not show them in such a form, and because it makes known the nature of causes and states having causes for the path-factors and their associated states by way of meaning.

That ultimate reality (paramattha) towards which the mind flows, leans, and inclines should be understood as the object-predominant (ārammaṇādhipati) of that mind. One who reflects after first knowing with the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa) is called "one who reflects with that cetopariyañāṇa." The phrase "here also" refers to this Commentary's words, or to the passage of rejection in the Paṭṭhāna where the predominant condition (adhipati-paccaya) of other states is not mentioned while excluding the path, etc. "Only this meaning" refers to the meaning "excluding one's own path-fruition." By the word "vīmaṃsādhipateyya" (predominance of investigation), the conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati) is indicated through the principal predominance. Since such an indication is merely a demonstration of the method, other similar conascent path-predominances are also indicated. Therefore, it should also be applied as "vīriyādhipateyya" (predominance of energy). Indeed, this vīriyādhipateyya is also spoken of by way of meaning.

One's own nature is called "individual existence" (attabhāva). For beings who live for many thousands of aeons (kappa), the result of a kamma that has gained an opportunity arises after the passing of a thousand aeons. Or, whatever kamma will gain an opportunity even after a thousand aeons is also considered a kamma that has gained an opportunity; thus it is said with reference to its own result (vipāka). "It is not that it does not exist" means it is not that it has not yet arisen. Because they are included in the three moments such as arising (uppāda), they are spoken of by the phrase "arisen states" (uppādino dhammā); thus it is said, "What is called arisen states (uppādino dhammā) are the states that have come into being." The "self" (atta) referred to as the immaterial (arūpa) means the immaterial life-continuum (arūpa-bhavaṅga). Therein, the conventional term "self" arises by way of meaning, consisting of the perception of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-saññā), and so on.

If the kamma that is being accumulated were to give all its results, and if one considers that kamma which has not yet gained an opportunity also gives results, and kamma that has already matured also gives results again, then all results would have to come from a single kamma, and there would be no opportunity for other kammas to give results.
167:
Because it would be pointless, or because there would be no opportunity even for its arising, or [no opportunity] for the giving of the result of a kamma that has already arisen. Alternatively, if it were possible for a kamma that has not yet found an opportunity to produce its result even in the absence of other conditions such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), then there would be no opportunity for the other apacayagāmi-kamma (the Path kamma) which eliminates other conditions like ignorance and craving and brings about the end of kamma. This means that even if the Path is developed, there would be no efficacy for the Path because kamma would still ripen even without other conditions like ignorance. Or, because there should always be the occurrence of the result (vipāka), there would be no opportunity for the occurrence of anything other than the result. "Taṃ pana" refers to the kamma that has been accumulated (āyūhita). This statement should be understood as being initiated to show that by the ripening of kamma with certain results, it also causes the result of kamma with uncertain results that has found an opportunity. The eight attainments (samāpatti) are said to be "certain results" (dhuvavipāka) because they definitely ripen, having a nature that is not abandoned due to the absence of powerful (opposing) kamma and the absence of the development of the Path of Arahantship. Why is "that which has not arisen" (anuppanna) mentioned when speaking of accumulated kamma? Because the nature of the occurrence of the word "accumulated" (āyūhita) also exists in kamma that will be accumulated in the future.

In the word "upādinnā", it is not the meaning of being combined as "upa" and "ādinnā"; the word "upa" is merely a prefix (upasagga). Therefore, it is called "upādinnā" because it is an object of clinging (upādāna), or because it is taken up by clingings, or because it is taken up by others without misinterpretation through such grasping as "I have developed the Path, the Path has arisen for me," and so on. Alternatively, by the word "upādinnā", only those states that are not the Path and Fruit are meant; it should be understood that by other words (such as internal, etc.), the states of the Path and Fruit are also meant.

## The explanation of the Summary of the Triplets (Tika-nikkhepa-kathā) is finished.
## The explanation of the Summary of the Couplets (Duka-nikkhepa-kathā)

"Mettāyanavasena" means by way of spreading loving-kindness (mettā). It should be understood that although it should be said as "mettayanavasena," it is said with a long vowel (lengthened). Loving-kindness (mettā) or affection (medana) is called mettāyana, and such a state occurs by way of affection (sineha). "Anudayati" should be said as "anudāti," but it is said as "anuddā" by inserting the letter "d" (as an augment). "Anuddāyanākāro" is the mode of protecting. Protecting itself is called "dāyanā." "Anuddāyitassa" means of the (mind) that has arisen through protecting. Knowledge of suffering (dukkhe ñāṇa) occurs in these four times: at the time of hearing when one hears "birth is also suffering," etc.; at the time of contemplating when one contemplates through impermanence, etc.; at the time of penetration when one destroys delusion regarding this (truth of suffering) by means of the Path; and at the time of reviewing when one reviews after having penetrated.
168:
The intense attachment of the mind is called the mind's sārāga (intense lust). "Gijjhanti" means they greatly desire. "Sañjanti" means they bind so as to be entangled. It is called "laggana" (attachment) because of the sense of restraint, as in being stuck so as not to escape, or because of the sense of hanging on. In various existences such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), it pulls by way of being a condition for rebirth for the sake of the arising of resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāmakkhandha) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattā-rūpa). The mind of that being runs to another existence and arises. The various fluctuations of craving and its deep involvement in objects are simply the occurrence of craving by way of the 108 modes of craving, and so on.

"Saritāni" are (minds) that are moistened by way of lust (rāga). They are smooth and sticky by way of the joy (pīti) associated with that lust. "Visatā" means extensive. They are spread out by way of pervading the states in the three planes, such as form, etc. In the previously mentioned word "visatā," the letter 't' is changed to 'ṭ' to say "visaṭā." "Visālā" means vast. "Visakkati" means it moves all around the objects, or it means it endures. For one who is stained by lust endures even being kicked with a foot by the object of lust (woman or man). They say that receding or fluctuating is "visakkana." It is called "visamvādikā" (deceptive) because it takes the five aggregates, which are impermanent, etc., as permanent, etc., and thus causes deviation. "Visamharati" means, seeing the advantages in the cords of sensual pleasure in various ways, it withdraws or contracts the mind from occurring towards renunciation (nekkhamma) in various modes. Alternatively, "visa" means suffering (dukkha), and it carries that suffering. It is called "visamūlā" (poison-rooted) because it is the cause of kamma that produces suffering. Or, it is called "visamūlā" because this craving has the root of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). It is called "visaphalā" (poison-fruited) because this craving has the result of suffering, being the origin of suffering. Since one can only enjoy suffering such as visible forms, etc., through craving, and cannot enjoy the Deathless Nibbāna, that craving is called "visaparibhogā" (poison-enjoyment). In all these terms, the formation of the words should be understood by way of linguistics (nirutti). To show which meaning is primary among these, the phrase "visatā vā panā," etc., is said again. "Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ" refers to the round of rebirths where human existence, deva existence, etc., arise.

By way of "paṇidhānaka" means by way of placing the mind on objects such as visible forms, etc. Although other living relatives also exist because of craving, those relatives can also become non-relatives. But craving is a relative that is always relied upon; therefore, it is called "pāṭiyekko bandhu" (a unique kinsman). Because of "asana" means because of pervading and because of consuming. Both these meanings are shown by the phrase "ajjhottharaṇato," etc. By way of "āsīsana" means by way of desiring and longing. "By another mode" means by way of the mode showing that jappanā and jappitatta are not different from jappā (craving). "It overwhelms the mind" means it robs and destroys the wholesome mind. "Mārapāsa" (Mara's snare): lust is called Mara's snare because it is captured by Mara.

By saying that (anger) arisen towards formations (saṅkhāra) does not create a specific path of kamma (kammapatha), it is understood that groundless anger (aṭṭhānakopa) arisen towards beings can create a path of kamma. "He did not do me a benefit..."
169:
“He did not work for my benefit in the past, he does not work for it now, he will not work for it in the future; he did not work for the harm of my dear and beloved one in the past, he does not work for it now, he will not work for it in the future; he did not work for the harm of my disliked and unloved one in the past, he does not work for it now, he will not work for it in the future”—anger arising in this way is appropriate to be called unjustified anger (aṭṭhāna-kopa) because it arises in what is not a ground. Āghātento means harassing or destroying (hananto). The statement “The fault of repetition (punarutti-dosa) has been avoided” is said because the words dosa (anger/fault) and paṭivirodha (opposition) appear twice. Alternatively, paṭivirodha is mentioned first to specify paṭigha (impingement), and dosa is mentioned to specify padosa (corrupt anger) and so on. Later, dosa is mentioned to specify dussana (the act of offending) and so on, and paṭivirodha is mentioned to specify virodha (opposition). Therefore, there is no fault of repetition.

In the Matika Uddesa, which shows only the existence of dhammas without yet extracting their distinctions, the inquiry is made using the plural number because it was pointed out with the plural number without distinction: “Which are the unconditioned states (appaccaya-dhammā)?” This is because the Uddesa (brief instruction) and Pucchā (question) are made according to the wish of a person who does not yet know the dhammas by way of their nature, number, or distinction. Therefore, they are briefly pointed out and questioned without making distinctions. For the purpose of showing that there are no unconditioned states beyond the unconditioned element (asankhata-dhātu), and based on the time when the beings to be enlightened did not yet know before the Niddesa (detailed exposition), that single unconditioned state is shown, and the conclusion is made using only the plural “ime” (these).

“Are there none? Because they do not exist, are they not taught?”—the construction should be made thus. The absence of a fixed rule that “mind-consciousness knows only this object” is called vavatthānābhāva (absence of definition). Since the Pali text states that only the objects known by eye-consciousness etc. are “cognizable by the eye” (cakkhādi-viññeyya), it should be considered that the states known by mind-consciousness are also “cognizable by the mind” (mano-viññeyya); thus, the Commentary states “What then by mind-consciousness?” and so on. The phrase “cognizable by some, not cognizable by others” should be applied by distinguishing the sense-sphere mind-consciousness (kāmāvacara-manoviññāṇa) by way of objects and so on. Indeed, sense-sphere states are not cognizable by sense-sphere mind-consciousness that has fine-material sphere objects etc., nor by that associated with fine-material lust (rūpa-rāga) etc.; they are cognizable by other types of mind-consciousness. Similarly, among sense-sphere objects, the cognizability or non-cognizability of certain sounds etc. by mind-consciousness having visible objects etc. should be applied. Likewise, it should be applied by way of the distinction of doors (dvāra). Alternatively, since the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata-santīraṇa) takes only agreeable objects, other objects are not cognizable by it. In this way, it should be applied as appropriate in all cases, such as in the wholesome resultant and unwholesome resultant accompanied by equanimity. Fine-material sphere objects etc. are not cognizable by sense-sphere resultants etc.; some...
170:
...are cognizable by immaterial sphere states (arūpāvacara); this should be applied because it follows the sequence. The statement “because it is not cognizable by Nibbāna” is said merely referring to the possibility of the meaning of the phrase “not cognizable by some,” not because Nibbāna is a mind-consciousness that follows the sequence. The phrase “lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure” is said by way of the excellent (ukkaṭṭha) method. It would be appropriate to say that all greed, excluding the taint of existence (bhavāsava), is the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava). Lust associated with the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) is called “bhavāsava” in the Commentary because it is associated with the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi). However, in the Pali, it is stated that bhavāsava arises only in consciousness dissociated from views (diṭṭhigata-vippayutta). That lust also deserves to be the taint of sensual desire. The taints of sensual desire etc., which are the causes of suffering in the present life and in the future life, are also stated in two ways.

In the exposition of the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava-niddesa), the term “in the senses” (kāmesu) can mean in the objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) of the three planes, which are the objects of sensual lust, lust for views, and so on. Indeed, all that craving arising in those objective sensualities does not fail to receive names such as “desire for sensuality” (kāmacchanda). The desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) arises even in the unwholesome, but the desire for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda) does not. Although the grasping of “the soul is one thing, the body is another” occurs only in the aggregates of clinging, it does not stay in matter... or consciousness; because it takes the soul as something different from those aggregates, it becomes the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). For one who takes a certain self such as Brahmā as “it exists” by way of permanence, and others as “it does not exist” by way of impermanence, the partial-eternalism view (ekacca-sassata-diṭṭhi) “it both exists and does not exist” occurs. For one who rejects all questions, saying “it is not so” when asked “does it exist?” and “it is not so” when asked “does it not exist?”, it is the eel-wriggling view (amarā-vikkhepa-diṭṭhi). Amarā means non-interruption, or it means a view of wavering like the amara fish. Because it is said that lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is the taint of sensual desire, it rejects the status of kāmāsava for the lust and lust for views arising in the mansions etc. of the Brahmās. If there were greed liberated from the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence, when that greed arises in consciousness dissociated from views, the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) associated with it should be called “dissociated from taints” (āsava-vippayutta), just like the delusion (moha) associated with displeasure, doubt, and restlessness. It should be said: “The delusion arising in the four types of greed-rooted consciousness dissociated from views may be associated with taints or dissociated from taints.” It is said: “The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight types of greed-rooted consciousness,” and “Dependent on the taint of sensual desire, the taint of views...”
171:
According to the Paṭṭhāna text, 'avijjāsavo' (the taint of ignorance), it cannot be said that greed (rāga) associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi) is not the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava). The meaning is that the defilements (kilesa) should be taken according to their sequence. Since the teaching of the taints (āsava) has the purpose of showing the defilements to be abandoned, when those taints are presented for the sake of abandonment, they should be taken according to the sequence of the defilements to be abandoned, and likewise, the paths (magga) that abandon them should also be taken.

'Paṭhamakamānabhājanīye' (In the first analysis of conceit) refers to the analysis of the conceit 'I am superior' (seyyo’hamasmī). In that (first analysis), it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'A certain person arouses conceit on account of birth, or lineage, or being of a good family, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or Vedic study, or occupation, or craft, or branch of knowledge, or learning, or eloquence, or any other ground. Such conceit, imagining... and the desire of the mind for a banner (ketukamyatā) exists.' This refers to the analysis of the conceit of superiority (seyyamāna) without specifically considering the individual differences that occur among the superior, the equal, and the inferior; thus it is said, 'One conceit is said to arise in three types of persons.' This should be understood as an example, for it is stated not only in the first analysis of conceit but also in the second and third analyses. Alternatively, the analysis of the three types of conceit taught without depending on the person is called the 'first analysis of conceit.' The analysis of the nine types of conceit taught by considering the person, such as 'the conceit that I am superior,' is the second analysis of conceit. This is because that collection of conceit is the second or third relative to the collection of conceit taught without considering the person. However, in the aforementioned second analysis of conceit, it is said, 'Three types of conceit arise in each person'; the term 'first analysis of conceit' is used here to show the similarity with the explanation given in this commentary. Since that very conceit is mentioned here, the meaning stated there (in the first analysis) is applicable. 

'Mānakaraṇavasena' means by way of performing the act of conceit such as 'superior.' 'Aparāpare upādāya' (depending on successive ones) is said with reference to the meaning that preceding conceits, by acting as a strong dependence (upanissaya), cause subsequent conceits to arise and become greatly uplifted. Because the mind of 'desire for a banner' (ketukamyatā) reaches a state of being greatly uplifted, it is specifically qualified by the mind (citta).

'Khiyyana' (complaining/grumbling) is the manifestation of intolerance. 'Mānana' (honoring) means the act of making something dear with the mind; such a form of worship is called 'mānana.' 'Issākaraṇavasena' means by way of the act of intolerance toward gains and so forth.
172:
The phrase 'ariyasāvakā' (noble disciples) is stated to show the absence of stinginess (macchariya) regarding the Dhamma of penetration (paṭivedha), meaning that only noble disciples have the penetration of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, and they are not stingy about that penetration. 'Gantha' refers to the Pali scriptures. 'Kathamagga' refers to the continuity of the Commentary (Atthakathā). 'Dhammantara' means corrupting the Dhamma such as wholesome states, and due to one's own fickleness, making the words spoken by the Tathāgata like the words spoken by sectarians, thereby mixing them with unwholesome states and so forth. 'Attānaṃ āvikatvā' means revealing oneself; making oneself known as having one quality (such as pure bodily conduct) while actually possessing another (such as impure conduct). 'Yo pana' refers to a sectarian or a householder who, not wishing to see the faults of their own doctrine due to ignorance or dogmatic attachment, is called 'viviccha' (one who does not wish to spread/disclose); the state of such a person is 'veviccha.'

'Anādara' (disrespect) refers to one who lacks respect in giving due to stinginess. Taking rice with a ladle is called 'kaṭacchuggāha'; it is called 'kaṭacchuggāha' (stinginess) because it is like taking rice with a ladle. Indeed, just as taking rice with a ladle does not spread the rice, so too stinginess does not wish to share (spread) places and so forth with others. Alternatively, it is called 'gāha' because rice is taken with this ladle; the ladle itself is the means of taking rice, hence 'kaṭacchuggāha.' Just as that ladle has a curved tip and does not spread, so too is stinginess. The mind that is clutched and closed is 'aggahita'; that state is the stinginess called 'aggahitatta.' This should be applied to the characteristic of grasping one's own success by way of the occurrence: 'Let places and so forth be mine alone, whether shared with others or not,' and the characteristic of hiding one's own success by way of the occurrence: 'Let it not belong to another.' The statement 'wishing to take what belongs to another' should be understood as being said to show that stinginess is a strong dependence (upanissaya) for greed (lobha) that desires another's property. If that statement were a description of the occurrence of stinginess, then the characteristic of taking another's success should also have been mentioned.

Regarding the difference between covetousness (abhijjhā) and sensual lust (kāmarāga), there could be the state of being two taints (kāmāsava and bhavāsava) or the state of being a single taint. Since there can be no covetousness that is not a taint, the existence of greed that is not a taint (no-āsava lobha) should be investigated. This is because the seventh and ninth questions—'States that are both taints and not taints are a condition by way of root-condition for a state that is a taint, and for states that are both taints and not taints'—do not exist (in the Paṭṭhāna). In the counting, it is stated as 'seven by way of root' (hetuyā satta), not 'nine.' If there were greed that is not a taint in greed associated with wrong view, the seventh and ninth questions would have received answers, and the counting would have to be stated as 'nine by way of root.' If there were greed that is not a taint in greed dissociated from wrong view, it would lead to the fault previously shown.
173:
## In the Explanation of the Hindrance of Sensual Desire

In the case of "in sensual pleasures" (kāmesu), it refers to all objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) associated with taints (sāsava) occurring in the three planes of existence. Indeed, all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa). For this reason, its occurrence in the formless realm (āruppa) is stated: "Dependent on a hindrance, a hindrance arises, not by way of pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya). In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of restlessness (uddhacca-nīvaraṇa) and the hindrance of ignorance (avijjā-nīvaraṇa) arise. In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thina-middha-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of restlessness, and the hindrance of ignorance arise" (in the Paṭṭhāna).

The mind supporting the postures (iriyāpathūpatthambhakacitta) refers to the fifty-eight types of consciousness that support the postures. Among them, the mind accompanied by strong sloth and torpor is said to be "unable to maintain the posture." *Olīyati* means slumping or sagging.

*Onayhati* means covering or overwhelming. Internal obstruction (antosamorodha) occurs either by preventing occurrence in various objects or by preventing expansion. "Of some" (ekaccānaṃ) refers to trees such as the Sirīsa. [The intention is:] (The experience of pleasure and the realization of Nibbāna) should occur through the material body alone; if so, the experience of pleasure and the realization of Nibbāna would become material properties. Therefore, the word "of the body" (kāyassa) does not establish the state of being matter. The mental body (nāmakāya) does not sleep; this statement refers to the sagging of the limbs and organs that have reached a state of heaviness in the material body due to matter originating from sloth and torpor, which is intended as "sleep" (soppa), and not the bhavanga-continuum devoid of waking consciousness. Because it is the result of that sloth and torpor, in order to show torpor (middha) like a faculty (indriya) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), just as gender (liṅga) etc. are mentioned in the explanation of faculties (indriya-niddesa), so too sleep (soppa) etc. are mentioned in the explanation of torpor (middha-niddesa). This is the meaning.

Since there is no internal obstruction in the material body (rūpakāya), it should be understood that this obstruction is taught regarding the mental body. Shrouding (onāha) and enveloping (pariyonāha), which are taught along with that obstruction, also [refer to the mental body]. Alternatively, the state of expansion or non-expansion of the material body does not exist by its own nature; when the mental body expands, [the material body] is light, and when it does not expand, it is heavy. Thus, through the state of non-expansion, shrouding (onāhana) etc. belong only to the mental body; therefore, shrouding etc. are understood only in the mental body. Hence it is said: "Matter is not the shrouding of the mental body... it is." For, like the state of being an obstacle, the state of being a shroud etc. belongs only to the mental body. Another person (the objector), not knowing the intention and seeing the shrouding of material forms by material forms like clouds etc., says "Is it not that..." (nanu ca) etc. If the state of shrouding etc. of matter were established in this way, then the obstruction of the immaterial...
174:
...would not be. The meaning is: since the obstruction of matter is seen in the construction of dams etc., obstruction (āvaraṇa) would not exist for the immaterial (arūpa).

Considering that drinking fermented and distilled intoxicants is unwholesome, its status as an impurity (upakkilesa) is appropriate. Since the addiction to the practice of drinking intoxicants, which is the basis for negligence (pamādaဋ္ဌāna), is also unwholesome, its status as a weakener of wisdom is appropriate. Nevertheless, granting the other's view, the status of intoxicants as an impurity and a weakener of wisdom is stated by way of metonymy (attributing the result to the cause), because they are the cause of impurities and the weakening of wisdom. To show this, he said: "No, because of the explanation of the cause." "Just so" (evam-eva kho) means: just as gold is defiled by five impurities—iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver—and being defiled by these five impurities, gold is neither soft, nor wieldy, nor radiant, but is brittle and does not properly lend itself to craftsmanship; just so. "Because of the explanation of the cause" means because of the explanation of the causal status of the impurities and the weakening of wisdom; the meaning is: because of the explanation of the result in the cause. The intention of the commentator is that torpor (middha) itself is a defilement and has already been pointed out in the explanations of impurities.

When showing the association with hindrances only after they have become hindrances, the undertaking (ārambha) is not for the purpose of showing the status of being a hindrance, but rather for the purpose of showing the association with hindrances of sloth and torpor whose status as a hindrance is already established. Therefore, it is not appropriate to speak of non-association according to whatever opportunity is obtained. Just as the two modes of staying and moving are stated according to whatever opportunity is possible in the case of shells, mollusks, etc., there is no such statement as "the hindrance of sloth and torpor is both associated and dissociated" which might occur according to opportunity. "Because of the statement of the impossibility of being mind-born" means because of the statement "due to being abandoned" (cattattā) etc., which expresses the impossibility of sloth and torpor being mind-born (cittaja) at the moment of Jhana. Alternatively, it means the impossibility is revealed by the statement "due to being abandoned" etc.

"But in the case of sensual pleasures... it is well seen." By this, he speaks of the abandoning of ignorance (aññāṇa/moha) regarding the danger of sensual pleasures. "Abandoning in that matter" (taṃ tattha pahānaṃ) means "abandoning in that material form"; the word "that" (taṃ) is used in reference to "abandoning" (pahāna), or it means that removal. By that, he shows only the fact that matter is not to be abandoned. However, in passages such as "having abandoned six states," no other way is stated than showing that torpor is not to be abandoned. The meaning is: "Just as the six states and the five hindrances are indeed to be abandoned, it is not stated that matter is indeed to be abandoned."

They are called obstacles (āvaraṇa) because they obstruct the arising of the wholesome. They are called hindrances (nīvaraṇa) because they prevent the arising of the wholesome. They are called overpowers of the mind (cetaso ajjhāruha) because they overwhelm and mount the mind. The function of being an obstacle etc. is appropriate only for immaterial states (arūpa). The function of being a maker of blindness (andhakaraṇa) etc. is likewise appropriate only for immaterial states. Among these four terms beginning with "Bhikkhus, the hindrance of sloth and torpor," the subsequent term...
175:
Just as it is taught that the six dhammas and the five hindrances are things that "should be abandoned" (pahatabbāni) because they are indeed to be abandoned, it is meant that although form (rūpa) is also to be abandoned, it is not taught in that way as "should be abandoned."

To show the Suttas already mentioned by the phrase "and by other Suttas," the words beginning with "tathā hi" are spoken. They are called obstructions (āvaraṇa) because they block the arising of wholesome states. They are called hindrances (nīvaraṇa) because they prevent [wholesome states]. They are called "overpowering the mind" (cetaso ajjharūhā) because they overpower and ascend upon the mind. The function of obstruction and the like, as well as the function of making blind (andhakaraṇa) and the like, is appropriate only for mental phenomena (arūpa). Among those four terms, each subsequent term explains the meaning of the preceding one. The suffering of saṃsāra is called distress (vighāta); because it produces that suffering, it is called "belonging to the side of distress" (vighātapakkhika). Since the overpowering of the mind, its arising through unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), and the state of being a mass of unwholesome states can only occur in mental phenomena, torpor (middha) is purely a mental phenomenon.

Having eaten unallowable food such as a group meal (gaṇabhojana) while perceiving it as allowable, and later realizing it was unallowable, someone feels remorse (vippaṭisāra). Also, by not performing blameless acts such as seeing monks or worshipping a cetiya while perceiving them as blameworthy, or after performing them, some faithless person feels remorse. "Vatthu" means the root (mūla). "Evarūpaṃ" means having such a variety by way of the root. In the yevāpanaka dhammas, the term "kukkucca" (worry/remorse) has the same meaning as previously stated: "what is done badly is kukata; the state of that kukata is kukkucca." The mode of worrying (kukkuccāyanākāro) is the mode of producing, performing, or the occurrence of worry. By this, worry is shown as an action or state. The arising of thought as "is it allowable or not?" is indeed what is called kukkucca in the Vinaya.

It should be understood that restlessness (uddhacca) and worry (kukkucca) are taught together because of their common function of distracting the mind. It should be understood that the abandoning of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) by the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmimagga) is stated by way of the excessive hindrance of sensual desire. If there were greed (lobha) that was not a hindrance, it would have to be said that "a dhamma that is not a hindrance is a condition for a dhamma that is a hindrance by way of root-condition (hetu-paccaya)," but this was not said. Also, in the counting section (gaṇanāvāra), it is only said "four by way of root-condition," not "nine." Therefore, since all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire, the statement that it is abandoned by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) is appropriate.

"Kāmo ca" refers also to the defilement of sensuality (kilesakāma). "The subsequent view grasps the preceding view" means grasping the preceding wrong view as "eternal" (sassata). Or, the subsequent view, arising in the same manner as the preceding wrong view, makes that preceding view firm and is said to grasp it. The bovine moral conduct and bovine vows (gosīla-govata) and so on refer to such wrong views.
176:
"Abhinivesato" means because of the state of firm adherence or due to firm adherence. "Attavādamattameva" means that since a self (atta) does not truly exist, it refers only to this word "self" (atta). "Upādiyanti" means they grasp firmly. How do they grasp? As "self." Those who firmly adhere to the notion of "self" grasp it by making only the word firm. Thus it is said that they grasp only the mere doctrine of self. Alternatively, by the phrase "attavādamattaṃ," it refers to the mere basis of speech. Because the self does not truly exist, they grasp only the basis of speech as "self."

By the word "dinnaṃ," the volition of giving (dānacetanā) is meant. Because that giving has no fruit, it is rejected as not being giving at all, like a mere form. A sacrifice similar to the sacrifice of King Mahāvijitāvī is a great sacrifice (mahāyāga). Inviting and making an offering or giving is called "āhunaṃ." Performing hospitality for guests is called "pāhunaṃ." Giving for the sake of auspiciousness in weddings and so on is called an auspicious act (maṅgalakiriyā). When it is said that one who stays in the next world (para-loka) holds this world to be "non-existent," it means that the next world is in relation to this world, and this world is in relation to the next world, by way of going and coming. It should be understood that because there is no coming from the next world to this world, and because there is annihilation (ucchinda) in that very existence, one who stays in the next world mentally holds this world to be "non-existent." This wrong view does not occur only to one born in the next world. The same method applies to the phrase "staying in this world" (idhaloke thito). Or else, the meaning here is: "there is no such thing as this world or the next world as a place of wandering, because there is no wandering in saṃsāra, as there is annihilation in each respective existence." Falling from a preceding life into a subsequent life is called "upapāta"; those who have the habit of such falling are "opapātikā" (spontaneously born beings). Since they are those who pass away and are born, it is said: "one holds that there are no beings who pass away and are born." "Anulomappaṭipadā" is the practice of virtue and so on that is in conformity with Nibbāna.

By the phrase "nippadesato gahito" (taken without exception), the partiality (sappadesatta) mentioned in the Asavagocchaka—due to not including greed and the greed for views regarding the celestial trees (kapparukkha) of the Brahmas—and in the Nīvaraṇagocchaka—by showing that sensual desire is to be abandoned by the Path of Non-Returning—is refuted. By the word "arahattamaggena," it should be understood that abandoning by the four paths is meant. For delusion (moha) and so on, which have not been attenuated by the preceding paths, cannot be abandoned by the Path of Arahantship alone.

"Nirati-atthena" means by way of being devoid of rapture (pīti) or devoid of strong attachment (nikanti). This is because beings do not delight in painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). By the syllable "ava," two meanings are stated: the meaning of plunging into (ogāha) and the meaning of downward (adho).
177:
The dust of delusion associated with doubt is 'with dust' (saraṇa) along with the dust of lust associated with wrong view, in the sense of being abandoned. The dust of delusion associated with restlessness is 'with dust' along with the dust of lust known as lust for form and lust for the formless. However, in the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta (M. Ni. 3.333), it is said: 'That devotion to the pleasure of sensual happiness for one who has happiness through sensual rebirth is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; this state is accompanied by suffering, accompanied by vexation, accompanied by despair, and accompanied by fever; it is a wrong practice. Therefore, this state is with dust (saraṇa).' Because of such words, the state of wrong practice, which has the nature of resultant suffering, vexation, despair, and fever, is understood as 'saraṇa'. Thus, through these [terms like] suffering, etc., the state of being 'with dust' for all unwholesome states is established.

## Explanation of the Suttantika Duka Nikkhepa

'Vivecitattā' means because of being made separate, because of being clearly shown. 'Destroys without remainder' means that a thunderbolt (vajira) destroys the place where it falls without remainder, so that it cannot return to its original state.

'Tappati' means one has remorse, or one grieves repeatedly.

In the word 'ahaṃ' (I), the meaning is understood because of the word 'ahaṃ' followed by the word 'iti'; that meaning is well-spoken or uttered. Otherwise, if the meaning of the term (the five aggregates) being shown by the spoken word were 'saṅkhā' (reckoning) and so on, then all wholesome states, etc., would become 'adhivacana' (designation) and so on. 'Bhāva' is said to be a synonym for 'satta' (being), or it is a name for 'dhātu' (element). By this much word 'datta', the designation of beings (sattapaññatti) is shown, and to show other derivative designations (upādāpaññatti), the words 'mañca' (couch) and so on are spoken. The name-word 'ahaṃ' is understood by the speaker and the listener through the perception (saññā) previously acquired, by way of manifesting the meaning. Since it is impossible to know that meaning without knowing that word, the name is specifically called 'sammaññā' because it is known. It is known by the power of perceiving that 'ahaṃ' is the name for this meaning; it is well-known, it is manifest, therefore it is called 'sammaññā'. 'Paññāpīyati' (it is designated) means it is established that this word 'ahaṃ' is the name for this meaning. 'Vohārīyati' means it is called or conventionally used. 'Uddheyya' means it should be extracted. 'Even from a thousand names' means even by many thousands of names. A name that has the nature of occurring spontaneously is called an 'opapātika nāma'.
178:
Because it is made, it is called 'kamma'; the name itself is called 'nāmakamma' because it is made. Likewise, it is 'nāmadheyya'. Indeed, the words 'karaṇa' (making) and 'ṭhapana' (establishing) also have the sense of 'kamma' (object). If they have the sense of instrument (karaṇa), then because the meaning is made, established, and designated by this name as 'having such a name', it is called 'karaṇa' and 'ṭhapana'. If they have the sense of state (bhāva), then the mere act of making known is called 'karaṇa' and 'ṭhapana'. 'Nāmanirutti' (name-language) and 'nāmabyañjana' (name-phrasing) mean simply 'name' (nāma). Indeed, it is not the mere distinction of meaning called 'earth-substance' that expresses or manifests; rather, it is the name-word 'pathavī' (earth) that expresses or manifests. Therefore, to prevent the status of language (nirutti) and phrasing (byañjana) for what is not a name, it is called 'nāmanirutti nāmabyañjana'. The same method applies to the term 'nāmābhilāpa' (name-utterance).

In this context, by the four terms 'saṅkhā', 'sammaññā', 'paññatti', and 'vohāra', the designation of meaning (atthapaññatti) is spoken of because it is what is designated (paññāpitabba). By the other terms, the designation of sound (saddapaññatti) is spoken of because it is what makes known (paññāpana). Among those designations, the former designation, which is devoid of the functions of arising and passing away and is established by worldly convention, is 'upādāpaññatti' (derivative designation). The latter designation is 'nāmapaññatti' (name designation). Teachers say that by that 'nāmapaññatti', the former 'atthapaññatti' and form (rūpa), etc., are made known, being grasped by the process of mind-door consciousness with previously acquired convention, occurring immediately after the process of ear-door consciousness.

If the meaning of this Pali and Commentary were according to the view of those teachers, it would contradict the words spoken in the Mātikā Commentary: 'Adhivacana is a name that occurs making only the word itself the primary object; abhilāpa, nirutti is a name spoken with a cause; paññatti is a name because of making known in various ways.' The reason is that for a designation devoid of the functions of arising and passing away, there is no occurrence based only on the word; such occurrence exists only in ultimate realities (paramattha) which have arising, etc. There is no name that is free from the word and the word's meaning that is extensively manifested and spoken of with a cause, nor is there a making known in various ways of a term's meaning that has an unmanifested ultimate nature.

Furthermore, the commentary statement about 'these two kinds of designations as mentioned' is not found. However, in the Puggalapaññatti Commentary, only the six kinds of designations such as 'vijjamanapaññatti' are mentioned. Among them: (1) 'rūpa', 'vedanā', etc., are designations of what exists (vijjamanapaññatti); (2) 'woman', 'man', etc., are designations of what does not exist (avijjamanapaññatti); (3) 'one with three-fold knowledge', 'one with six-fold higher powers', etc., are designations of what does not exist by what exists; (4) 'the sound of a woman', 'the sound of a man', etc., are designations of what exists by what does not exist; (5) 'eye-consciousness', 'ear-consciousness', etc., are designations of what exists by what exists; (6) 'a noble youth', 'a brahmin youth', etc., are designations of what does not exist by what does not exist. In this Puggalapaññatti Commentary, the two kinds of designations as mentioned...
179:
It can be understood that there are the aforementioned varieties. For the names of existing meanings such as form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), etc.—namely saṅkhā (description), samaññā (designation), paññatti (concept), vohāra (usage), nāma (name), nāmakamma (naming), nāmadheyya (name-giving), nirutti (language), byañjana (articulation), and abhilāpa (utterance)—are 'concepts of the existent' (vijjamānapaññatti). The names such as saṅkhā, etc., of non-existing meanings are also 'concepts of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti). Those names such as saṅkhā, etc., which occur by way of the relationship between the qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesitabba) of those two types (existent and non-existent), are the remaining four types of concepts.

If it is asked: "By the term 'concept of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti), are not both the 'derivative concept' (upādāpaññatti) which is made known, and the 'name concept' (nāmapaññatti) which makes it known, already stated? And by the other five types of terms, is it not only the 'name concept' as previously described that is stated?"

The answer is: No, because the meaning is not established. For even though there is a direct meaning that follows the previously mentioned Pali, the assertion that 'this meaning of these two types of concepts is stated by this Puggalapaññatti Commentary' cannot be established. If derivative concepts (upādāpaññatti) such as beings, chariots, pots, directions, time, kasiṇas, space, the object of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of cessation are 'concepts of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti), then by the very word 'concept of the non-existent', their non-existence is already stated; therefore, one should not say that such derivative concepts 'exist'.

Just as there is the status of 'concept of the non-existent' for non-existing things like beings because of the meaning to be made known, so too there must be the status of 'concept of the existent' for existing things like form (rūpa) because of the meaning to be made known. If that were the case, then the exposition of conceptual states (paññattidhamma), which is not distinct from the 'pathways of concepts' (paññattipatha), should be stated as 'all states are concepts'. Even if it is argued that the exposition of saṅkhā, etc., is for the purpose of showing the distinction between what is made known (paññāpitabba) and what makes it known (paññāpana), it still cannot be so. Since the status of being a 'pathway of concepts' for things to be made known has already been shown by such statements as 'one state falls within all states, all states fall within one state', the term 'pathway of concepts' (paññattipatha) should not be used, as the pathways of concepts are already expressed by the word 'concept' (paññatti) itself in the sense of things being made known. Nor can it be said that the exposition of saṅkhā, etc., is for the purpose of showing the distinction between the meaning to be made known and the name that makes it known, because the words saṅkhā, etc., are synonymous.

It has been stated: "Even that which a man considers as 'this is mine' is abandoned by him through death." In this context, it is said: "'Man' is a description (saṅkhā), a designation (samaññā) ... an utterance (abhilāpa)." Likewise, it is said: "'Māgaṇḍiya' is the name, the description, the designation of that brahmin." Apart from the grasping of convention (saṅketaggahaṇa)—such as 'this meaning has this name'—and the grasping of speech (vacanaggahaṇa)—such as 'form is Tissa'—there is no ability to make known any other meaning that has an unestablished nature. And those two (saṅketaggahaṇa and vacanaggahaṇa) are also incapable without concepts. If they were incapable of making known the meaning without a concept, they would also be incapable of making known the concept; thus, another concept would have to be stated for that concept, and another for that, leading to an infinite regress (anavatthā). If that were so, the understanding of meaning itself would not exist. Even if a convention exists as a concept, the grasping of the convention as 'this is the meaning of this speech' or 'this speech illuminates this meaning' would not be possible. In the grasping of a convention which is merely the arising of a perception (saññā), there is no benefit in imagining a convention that is independent of the word and its meaning.
180:
There is no benefit in imagining a convention that is independent of the word and its meaning. Through such Pali passages as: "The Blessed Buddha’s usage (vohāra) strikes the ears of worldly beings" (Kathāvatthu); "Ānanda, have you ever heard such a name (nāmadheyya) as Janavasabha before this?" (Dīgha Nikāya); and "Koṇḍañña, I, the Blessed One, make the name known" (Saṃyutta Nikāya), the status of concept as speech (vacana) is established. Therefore, the meaning should be scrutinized and accepted in a way that is not contradictory to the Pali and the Commentaries.

If beings and so forth are not 'concepts of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti), then what is called 'concept of the non-existent'? This meaning has already been explained: "The description ... utterance of non-existing beings and so forth is 'concept of the non-existent'." Since beings and so forth do not exist (in the ultimate sense), one should not say they "exist". As for those who say, "It is called 'non-existent' (avijjamāna) because it does not exist in another way, like form and so forth, but not because of total non-existence," that view has been refuted in the Hevatthikathā. Just because form is not feeling, it does not mean it is 'non-existent'. Similarly, if beings and so forth did exist, they should not be called 'non-existent' merely because they are not form and so forth.

In reality, while those forms, eye-bases, and so forth are occurring in various ways, a diverse perception (saññā) such as "being, woman, chariot, pot" arises, and designations (adhivacana) conforming to that perception also arise. Apart from those forms, eye-bases, and so forth, the 'meaning of the word' (vacanattha) which relies on the perception of 'being', 'chariot', etc., does not truly exist. Therefore, utterances such as 'being' and 'chariot' are called 'concepts of the non-existent' (avijjamānapaññatti). These terms are not called "falsehoods" (musā) because they occur by way of worldly designation (lokasamaññā). For that very reason, these utterances are called 'conventional truth' (sammutisacca). Although that 'meaning of the word' (vacanattha) does not exist by itself, it receives the name 'conceptual usage' (paññattivohāra) by the power of the existing speech (vacana). It is also called 'conventional truth' because it is a word-meaning that occurs by the power of the perception as it is grasped. In the Kathāvatthu, it is said: "Conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa) has only truth as its object, not anything else"; it should be understood that this was said with the intention that "the earth-kasiṇa, etc., and robes, etc., are included in conventional truth."

Because when form and so forth are occurring as a continuum, the grasping of 'being' and so forth—which occurs without discarding those forms by way of grasping them as a unity—takes as its object the 'being' or 'chariot' which does not exist in those aggregates or eye-bases, just as eye-consciousness takes form as its object. Therefore, it is said that such an object should not be spoken of in terms of being a 'limited object' (parittārammaṇa) and so forth. Similarly, based on what is grasped as a unity in the continuum of the group of aggregates, [it is said] "Spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta)..."
181:
The taking [of a person] as 'a person who is a bad friend' and the designation [thereof] occur. Because wholesome and unwholesome states arise for one who associates with the collection of aggregates—which is the basis for such grasping—with the perception of a 'person', it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: 'A person is also a condition by way of decisive support condition.' However, what is called a 'person' is not a reality (sabhāva) that truly exists. Therefore, just as the earth element is found when the water element and others are distinguished by the mind, a person is not found when the aggregates such as form are distinguished. In the Puggalakathā, the view of a person (puggaladiṭṭhi) is also prohibited. The Bhikkhunī Vajirā also said to Māra:

'Māra, why do you believe in a "being"? You have a wrong view.
This is a mere heap of conditioned formations; no "being" is found here.'

To show the occurrence of the designation of the word 'being', that same Bhikkhunī continued:

'Just as the word "chariot" occurs due to the assembly of parts,
So when the five aggregates exist, the convention "being" occurs.'

If a person does not exist, how can the grasping of a person have an object (sārammaṇatā)? The answer is because even a non-existent object can be grasped. In truth, the mind arises only by taking an object that is either imagined, recognized in the world, or a truly existing reality; thus it is said to have an object. The word 'sārammaṇa' (having an object) merely indicates that mind and mental factors cannot occur without an object; it does not indicate whether the object grasped by them is existent or non-existent. This is the decision of the teachers who completely follow the negation of the existence of [concepts] which are distinct from the conditioned and the unconditioned.

'Nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena' means by the nature of making its own name by itself without depending on anything else. That which makes a name for another depends on that other, and thus it is a name-making that depends on another, not the nature of [intrinsic] name-making. Therefore, the masses, relatives, and qualities that create common names and so on do not reach the state of 'nāma' (mentality). A person whose name is given by others (e.g., King Mahāsammata) also does not have the nature of name-making and thus does not exist as 'nāma'. However, because states like feeling (vedanā) are established by their own nature, the names like 'feeling' have the nature of name-making and are thus called 'nāma'. The illustration of earth (pathavī) and so on is intended only to show how 'nāma' is established by its own nature, not to show a general similarity in being 'nāma'. Because the word 'nāma' is well-known only in regard to formless phenomena (arūpadhamma), it is used only for those states and not for the earth element and so on; thus they are not 'nāma'. In the Mātikā, too, regarding earth and so on...
182:
It has already been stated that material phenomena such as earth do not reach the state of 'nāma'. The reason is that, while material phenomena occur in the form of a collection with names like 'hair' after discarding names like 'earth', formless phenomena (arūpadhamma) do not occur in the form of a collection called by another name after discarding names like 'feeling'. Alternatively, material phenomena like the eye and visible objects are manifest without a name because of their nature as that which manifests and that which is manifested. Formless phenomena are not like that. They are called 'nāma' because they have the nature of being grasped in connection with a name, like designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa). Impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa) is also called 'nāma' because it is not manifest without a name, unlike the eye and so on. This impingement-contact is included in 'nāma' either because it is a formless phenomenon, or because it shares the nature of other mental phenomena, or because it shares the nature of other types of contact. Here, the etymological definitions 'it is rūpa because it manifests (rūpayati)' and 'it is nāma because it makes a name (nāmayati)' should apply to the subsequent material phenomena and the preceding mental phenomena respectively. 'Rūpayati' means it manifests itself even without a name. 'Nāmayati' means it makes a name that manifests itself because it is not manifest without a name. Regarding the state of being an object-predominance condition, although materiality can be an object-predominance condition, it is not a condition with the extraordinary nature of 'bending' [the mind] like Nibbāna, which is the ultimate relief; therefore, only Nibbāna is called 'nāma'.

'For the purpose of showing the occurrence of the roots of the round (vaṭṭa)' means for the purpose of showing ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), which are the roots of the round for beings. In this context, 'samudācarati' means it occurs excessively or repeatedly; thus the root of the round itself is the occurrence (samudācāra). Since the occurrence of the roots of the round is shown by showing the roots themselves, it also means 'for the purpose of showing the occurrence of the roots of the round'.

Based on the specific grasping of each of the five aggregates as 'self' and 'world', it is said 'self and world'. Or, it is said 'self and world' by virtue of one who grasps one aggregate as self and another as the world which is his own utility, or one who grasps his own self as 'self' and another's self as 'world'. 'That will be' means the firm and wrong misapprehension that the five aggregates grasped in those two ways will exist.

The Dhamma to be practiced together is called 'sahadhamma'; the training rule (sikkhāpada) existing in that Dhamma is 'sahadhammika'. Because the word 'āyasam' is added to the word 'dovacassa' (which is in the sense of action/kamma) without any other meaning, it is said 'dovacassāyaṃ', meaning 'the act of one who is difficult to speak to'. Alternatively, the occurrence of being difficult to speak to is 'dovacassāyaṃ'. Speaking in opposition to what another has said is...
183:
Paṭāṇikagahaṇaṃ means taking up a position of contradiction against what others say. Living with respect and honor toward those worthy of respect due to virtues such as morality (sīla) is called garuvāsa. Living among those who are senior by birth, etc., and who should be listened to, is called sajeṭṭhakavāsa. Alternatively, those who should be feared are called garu, and those before whom one should feel shame are called jeṭṭhaka. The volition (cetanā) because of which one becomes difficult to speak to is considered to be dovacassatā (unruliness); thus, it is said, "it is only the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)."

1333. A name associated with the word "du" is called dunnamā. With the meaning that practicing by imitating from afar even without approaching the one to be emulated is sevanā (association), it is said, "bhajanā means approaching (upasaṅkamanā)." Sabbato bhāgena means (associating) through body, speech, and mind, both openly and privately.

1336. Vinaya refers to the Vibhaṅga and the Khandhakas. Since there is no one who reaches an offense (āpatti) before or after the moment of transgressing the basis (vatthu), one distinguishes the offense along with its basis. Therefore, it is said, "along with the basis... is called āpattikusalatā (skill in offenses)." Saha kammavācāya means (being together) with the Abbhāna-kammavācā and Tiṇavatthāraka-kammavācā, and with words such as "Venerable Sir, I have fallen into such and such an offense." In truth, one distinguishes the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from an offense only together with the formal act (kammavācā). Alternatively, since the cause of an offense is the basis (vatthu) and the cause of emergence from an offense is the formal act (kammavācā), it is stated as "along with the basis, along with the formal act" by way of knowing the effect together with its cause.

1338. This same meaning is stated here as "saha parikammena." Vuṭṭhānakapaññā refers to the preparatory wisdom (parikammapaññā) which is the cause for emerging from an attainment.

1340. All wisdom that takes the elements (dhātu) as its object is called dhātukusalatā (skill in elements). With the meaning that the wisdom knowing the acquisition and attention (uggahamanasikāra), which is a part of that wisdom, is manasikārakusalatā, the wisdom knowing the acquisition and attention is also mentioned in the preceding term. Alternatively, in the preceding term, the attention to the Pali text of the elements that has been memorized is called "manasikāra." Among those types of wisdom such as acquisition (uggaha), the wisdom that involves learning, attending, listening to the meaning of the Pali text of the elements, bearing it in mind by way of the text and the meaning, and knowing the definition by way of nature such as "this is called the eye-element" and by way of number as being eighteen, is called uggahapaññā, etc. In the subsequent term, those five kinds of wisdom are called "uggaha," and the attention by way of impermanence, etc., that occurs thereafter is called "uggahamanasikāra." Knowing that uggahamanasikāra means its occurrence. Alternatively, knowing the learning that has arisen as "this is such a learning" is called uggahajānana. Knowing the attention as "it should be produced in this way, and it has been produced in this way" is called manasikārajānana. Both of these...
184:
...is called manasikārakosalla (skill in attention). Both the knowledge of learning (uggaha) and the knowledge of attention (manasikāra) are meant by manasikārakosalla. Indeed, since learning is associated with attention, it is appropriate for it to receive the name "attention" (manasikāra). Both the object that should be attended to, such as the characteristic of impermanence, and the wisdom which is the means of attention, can be called attention. The knowledge that is skillful in these matters is called manasikārakusalatā (skill in attention).

By the words beginning with "tīsu pi vā," the state of that skill as learning (uggaha), etc., is stated. The wisdom of investigation (sammasanapaññā), when associated with the Path (magga), accomplishes the task of investigating by way of impermanence, etc., by abandoning the perception of permanence (niccasaññā), etc. Similarly, attention associated with investigation, when associated with the Path, accomplishes the task of attending by way of impermanence, etc. Therefore, it is said, "investigation and attention are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane." Knowing the state of being a cause for the produced states such as mental formations (saṅkhāra) from ignorance (avijjā), etc., in the form of "this arises because of this cause," shows the skill in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā).

Mango seeds and so forth are mentioned to show non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) inanimate objects. The eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth, which are of a different nature, unsuitable, and unable to produce the ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa), etc., are called "dissimilar conditions" (visabhāgapaccaya). The ear-consciousness and so forth, which cannot arise because of those eye-bases, etc., are called "states produced by dissimilar conditions" (visabhāgapaccayasamuppannadhamma). Alternatively, it is a dissimilar condition because it is a condition for the eye-consciousness which is of a different nature from the ear-consciousness. A state produced by the ear-base, which is a condition dissimilar to the eye-base, is called visabhāgapaccayasamuppanna.

In the exposition of rectitude (ajjavaniddesa), "ajjava, ajjavatā" simply means uprightness or the state of being upright. In the expositions of rectitude (ajjava) and gentleness (maddava), while explaining uprightness and softness, the term "nīcacittatā" (lowliness of mind) is specifically mentioned in the exposition of gentleness. In that exposition of gentleness, the mention of "mudutā" (gentleness) again after "nīcacittatā" is for the purpose of qualifying nīcacittatā. This is because inferior pride (omāna) is also a form of lowliness of mind, but it is not gentleness (mudutā).

Without reacting against the bad deeds and bad words of others, they endure them by taking them upon themselves. "Cittassa sakamanatā" means the mind's own natural state which is not perverted. Alternatively, taking the mental continuum as a single unit, it refers to the state of the mind accompanied by joy (pīti) that arises within that continuum. Alternatively, a person who has his own mind is called "attamana," and the state of such a person is attamanatā. To prevent the view of a person (puggaladiṭṭhi) that this attamanatā is the state of a being (satta), it is stated as "of the mind" (cittassa).
185:
By not performing what should be done with body and speech, and by delighting in what should not be delighted in, such as gold and silver, one also acts with the mind. Alternatively, it should be understood that this is stated in terms of the destruction of virtue, such as the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara).

On a tree with defects, lumps of resin or sprouted mushroom buds are called 'aṇḍaka'. Similarly, powder clumps or nodules that appear like eggs on a decaying tree with sapwood should also be understood as 'aṇḍaka'. Harsh speech that enters the ear like a lotus stalk rubbing against it should be regarded as 'kakkasā'. Speech that arises due to anger and is an accompaniment to that anger is called 'kodhasāmanta'. Just as a maiden grown up in a city is called 'porī', speech that is very delicate and soft like such a maiden is called 'porī'. In that word 'tattha', the connection of meaning can occur either with the verb stated as 'is spoken' or with that speech itself. By terms such as 'saṇhavācatā' (gentle speech), the volition (cetanā) that produces that speech is shown.

A hole caused by the non-attainment of material things (āmisa) is called an 'attainment-of-material-things hole' (āmisālābha-chidda). By the phrase 'dve yeva hi', only the two kinds of holes arising from the non-attainment of material things and the Dhamma, as previously mentioned, are intended. 'Gamanasabhāgena' means by a region suitable for the path to be traveled.
